sources.title: Toddler Won't Go to Sleep? 7 Tips to Help End Bedtime Battles
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (adapted from Sleeping Well: Tips for Parents of Babies and Young Children, © 2022 AAP)
sources.quote: to help your child understand that it will soon be time to go to sleep. Use this time to read them a story, put on quiet music, or give them a bath. It may be tempting to play with your child before bed. However, active play may make your child too excited to sleep. ... Make bedtime the same time every night. This helps your child know what to expect and helps them establish healthy sleep patterns. ... Let your child take a favorite thing to bed each night. ... Take care of child’s needs before bedtime so they don’t use them as reasons to avoid going to sleep. They may want a drink of water, a light left on, or the door left slightly open. ... Do not let your child sleep in the same bed with you. This can make it harder for them to fall asleep when they are alone. ... If they are safe and well, there is no need to go into their room while they sort out how to get themselves back to sleep. ... Keep in mind that children's main goal is to get you to appear. So if you appear for any reason, even just for "checking," they will expect you to come each time they call out.
sources.supports: Wind-down before bed (a story, quiet music, a bath; no active play), the same bedtime every night, a favourite object, meeting needs such as water, a light or an open door before bedtime, not sharing the parents' bed, not going back in when the child is safe and well, and that appearing for any reason (even checking) teaches the child to expect it. The page is about toddlers; we apply it to preschoolers. Fragments read through a page fetch, joined with ' ... '.

sources.title: Sleep and Your Preschooler
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Mary L. Gavin, MD; date reviewed June 2020)
sources.quote: Preschoolers need about 10 to 13 hours of sleep each day, including naps. Set regular bedtimes, wake-up times, and nap times for your child. If your child no longer takes naps, schedule some quiet time during the day. ... Having a regular bedtime routine and a quiet, comfortable bedroom can help your child sleep well. A relaxing routine may include going to the bathroom, changing into pajamas, brushing teeth, and reading a book. Turn off all screens at least 1 hour before bedtime ... Let your child choose a special toy or blanket to sleep with. Turn on a nightlight if your child is afraid of the dark. Do not lie with your child until they fall asleep ... Make sure your child gets plenty of exercise during the day. ... It’s common for kids this age to not want to go to bed ... If your child is afraid or gets very upset, go in and offer comfort. After comforting and returning your child to bed, say that it's time to go to sleep. Keep your visit short. If your child cries when you leave, wait a few minutes before going back in the room. If your child gets out of bed, calmly take them back to bed.
sources.supports: 10 to 13 hours of sleep, regular times, quiet time without a nap, a routine of bathroom, pajamas, teeth and a book, a quiet comfortable room, screens off an hour before, a special toy or blanket, a nightlight for fear of the dark, daytime exercise, that it is common not to want to go to bed, and the steps for calls and getting out of bed (wait a few minutes, comfort if afraid, short visit, say it is time to sleep, calmly take back to bed). Fragments read through a page fetch, joined with ' ... '.

sources.title: Toddler Won't Go to Sleep? 7 Tips to Help End Bedtime Battles
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (adapted from Sleeping Well: Tips for Parents of Babies and Young Children, © 2022 AAP)
sources.quote: to help your child understand that it will soon be time to go to sleep. Use this time to read them a story, put on quiet music, or give them a bath. It may be tempting to play with your child before bed. However, active play may make your child too excited to sleep. ... Make bedtime the same time every night. This helps your child know what to expect and helps them establish healthy sleep patterns. ... Let your child take a favorite thing to bed each night. ... Take care of child’s needs before bedtime so they don’t use them as reasons to avoid going to sleep. They may want a drink of water, a light left on, or the door left slightly open. ... Do not let your child sleep in the same bed with you. This can make it harder for them to fall asleep when they are alone. ... If they are safe and well, there is no need to go into their room while they sort out how to get themselves back to sleep. ... Keep in mind that children's main goal is to get you to appear. So if you appear for any reason, even just for "checking," they will expect you to come each time they call out.
sources.supports: Wind-down before bed (a story, quiet music, a bath; no active play), the same bedtime every night, a favourite object, meeting needs such as water, a light or an open door before bedtime, not sharing the parents' bed, not going back in when the child is safe and well, and that appearing for any reason (even checking) teaches the child to expect it. The page is about toddlers; we apply it to preschoolers. Fragments read through a page fetch, joined with ' ... '.

sources.title: Sleep and Your Preschooler
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Mary L. Gavin, MD; date reviewed June 2020)
sources.quote: Preschoolers need about 10 to 13 hours of sleep each day, including naps. Set regular bedtimes, wake-up times, and nap times for your child. If your child no longer takes naps, schedule some quiet time during the day. ... Having a regular bedtime routine and a quiet, comfortable bedroom can help your child sleep well. A relaxing routine may include going to the bathroom, changing into pajamas, brushing teeth, and reading a book. Turn off all screens at least 1 hour before bedtime ... Let your child choose a special toy or blanket to sleep with. Turn on a nightlight if your child is afraid of the dark. Do not lie with your child until they fall asleep ... Make sure your child gets plenty of exercise during the day. ... It’s common for kids this age to not want to go to bed ... If your child is afraid or gets very upset, go in and offer comfort. After comforting and returning your child to bed, say that it's time to go to sleep. Keep your visit short. If your child cries when you leave, wait a few minutes before going back in the room. If your child gets out of bed, calmly take them back to bed.
sources.supports: 10 to 13 hours of sleep, regular times, quiet time without a nap, a routine of bathroom, pajamas, teeth and a book, a quiet comfortable room, screens off an hour before, a special toy or blanket, a nightlight for fear of the dark, daytime exercise, that it is common not to want to go to bed, and the steps for calls and getting out of bed (wait a few minutes, comfort if afraid, short visit, say it is time to sleep, calmly take back to bed). Fragments read through a page fetch, joined with ' ... '.

sources.title: Toddler Won't Go to Sleep? 7 Tips to Help End Bedtime Battles
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (adapted from Sleeping Well: Tips for Parents of Babies and Young Children, © 2022 AAP)
sources.quote: to help your child understand that it will soon be time to go to sleep. Use this time to read them a story, put on quiet music, or give them a bath. It may be tempting to play with your child before bed. However, active play may make your child too excited to sleep. ... Make bedtime the same time every night. This helps your child know what to expect and helps them establish healthy sleep patterns. ... Let your child take a favorite thing to bed each night. ... Take care of child’s needs before bedtime so they don’t use them as reasons to avoid going to sleep. They may want a drink of water, a light left on, or the door left slightly open. ... Do not let your child sleep in the same bed with you. This can make it harder for them to fall asleep when they are alone. ... If they are safe and well, there is no need to go into their room while they sort out how to get themselves back to sleep. ... Keep in mind that children's main goal is to get you to appear. So if you appear for any reason, even just for "checking," they will expect you to come each time they call out.
sources.supports: Wind-down before bed (a story, quiet music, a bath; no active play), the same bedtime every night, a favourite object, meeting needs such as water, a light or an open door before bedtime, not sharing the parents' bed, not going back in when the child is safe and well, and that appearing for any reason (even checking) teaches the child to expect it. The page is about toddlers; we apply it to preschoolers. Fragments read through a page fetch, joined with ' ... '.

sources.title: Sleep and Your Preschooler
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Mary L. Gavin, MD; date reviewed June 2020)
sources.quote: Preschoolers need about 10 to 13 hours of sleep each day, including naps. Set regular bedtimes, wake-up times, and nap times for your child. If your child no longer takes naps, schedule some quiet time during the day. ... Having a regular bedtime routine and a quiet, comfortable bedroom can help your child sleep well. A relaxing routine may include going to the bathroom, changing into pajamas, brushing teeth, and reading a book. Turn off all screens at least 1 hour before bedtime ... Let your child choose a special toy or blanket to sleep with. Turn on a nightlight if your child is afraid of the dark. Do not lie with your child until they fall asleep ... Make sure your child gets plenty of exercise during the day. ... It’s common for kids this age to not want to go to bed ... If your child is afraid or gets very upset, go in and offer comfort. After comforting and returning your child to bed, say that it's time to go to sleep. Keep your visit short. If your child cries when you leave, wait a few minutes before going back in the room. If your child gets out of bed, calmly take them back to bed.
sources.supports: 10 to 13 hours of sleep, regular times, quiet time without a nap, a routine of bathroom, pajamas, teeth and a book, a quiet comfortable room, screens off an hour before, a special toy or blanket, a nightlight for fear of the dark, daytime exercise, that it is common not to want to go to bed, and the steps for calls and getting out of bed (wait a few minutes, comfort if afraid, short visit, say it is time to sleep, calmly take back to bed). Fragments read through a page fetch, joined with ' ... '.
